articles.title: Intelligence and personality traits do not predict inattentional blindness
articles.summary: Being smart, focused, or detail-oriented won’t stop you from missing unexpected objects hidden in plain sight. New research suggests that inattentional blindness is a universal quirk of the brain.

articles.title: PsyPost deploys audit program to track retracted and corrected scientific studies in its archive
articles.summary: When science corrects itself, science news should too. PsyPost has launched a custom Python program to daily audit its archive against Retraction Watch and Crossref, ensuring readers are promptly alerted when covered studies are retracted or flagged.

articles.title: Plant-based meat labels make food seem less masculine, study finds
articles.summary: A new study indicates that simply labeling a dish as "plant-based" makes meat-eaters view it as less masculine. This leads to more negative evaluations, especially among individuals who hold hostile sexist beliefs.

articles.title: The Drift Contract: Spectral Updates for Depth-Robust Local Learning
articles.summary: arXiv:2609.26811v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local learning trains each layer with its own auxiliary loss and no global backward pass, which makes layer updates structurally parallel. Two problems have kept it marginal: accuracy degrades as depth grows, and hyperparameters are fragile. We apply Muon-style spectral update geometry (momentum orthogonalization with spectral step scaling) to per-layer local updates, an intersection not previously studied. articles.summary: arXiv:2609.26826v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier benchmarks need tasks that current models cannot solve. But a task that no model solves is not automatically a hard task. articles.title: Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep
articles.summary: Caffeine may make sleep less restorative even when you fall asleep normally and stay in bed for eight hours, with EEG recordings revealing fewer of the slow brain waves associated with deep sleep. Individual sensitivity varies dramatically, meaning even caffeine consumed earlier in the day could affect nighttime recovery for some people.

articles.title: New study reveals that fluctuating—not just intense—brain signals play a hidden role in overeating
articles.summary: A recent study links inconsistent brain reward signals to higher body weight and erratic eating patterns. The research suggests that fluctuating neural responses, rather than consistently strong cravings, may drive overeating and certain eating disorders.

articles.title: Humor makes taboo words less distracting
articles.summary: Taboo words usually derail our focus, slowing down cognitive tasks. However, new research reveals a surprising twist: when profanity is funny, it becomes significantly less distracting, highlighting a fascinating link between humor, arousal, and attention.

articles.title: Sexual objectification does not erase the perceived humanity of OnlyFans creators, study suggests
articles.summary: People who sell explicit digital content online are heavily sexually objectified by observers, yet they are still viewed as capable individuals with free will. These findings challenge traditional psychological assumptions about objectification and dehumanization.

articles.title: More REM sleep linked to lower risk of 83 diseases
articles.summary: A large study tracking more than 95,000 people suggests that how you sleep may be linked to your risk of developing dozens of diseases. People who spent more time in REM sleep had lower risks of 83 conditions, including dementia, heart failure, and Parkinson’s disease, while more deep sleep was associated with lower risks of conditions such as type 2 diabetes and major depression.
